subject.title: Vlamertinghe: Passing the Chateau
subject.author: Edmund Blunden
subject.text:
'And all her silken flanks with garlands drest'-
But we are coming to the sacrifice.
Must those flowers who are not yet gone West?
May those flowers who live with death and lice?
This must be the floweriest place
That earth allows; the queenly face
Of the proud mansion borrows grace for grace
Spite of those brute guns lowing at the skies.

Bold great daisies' golden lights,
Bubbling roses' pinks and whites-
Such a gay carpet! poppies by the million;
Such damask! such vermilion!
But if you ask me, mate, the choice of colour
Is scarcely right; this red should have been duller.

title: The Quotation Mark Blunden Never Explains
standfirst: Edmund Blunden opens this poem inside someone else's quotation marks — a line lifted from Keats's frozen sacrifice on a Grecian urn — and then makes it move. The date in the title puts him on the road it describes the same month his own battalion went into the opening day of Passchendaele.

sections.heading: The Quotation Mark Blunden Never Explains
sections.body:
The poem's first words sit inside quotation marks Blunden never accounts for. "'And all her silken flanks with garlands drest'-" is the last line of the fourth stanza of Keats's [Ode on a Grecian Urn](https://poets.org/poem/ode-grecian-urn), where a priest leads a garlanded heifer toward an altar carved into an ancient vase: "Who are these coming to the sacrifice? / To what green altar, O mysterious priest, / Lead'st thou that heifer lowing at the skies, / And all her silken flanks with garlands drest?" Keats's sacrifice never actually happens. The urn freezes it a moment before the knife, and nothing painted onto pottery can die — that permanence is the whole argument of his ode, art outlasting the men who made it.

Blunden lifts only the last of those four lines, sets it down first with no explanation, and answers the question Keats leaves open: "But we are coming to the sacrifice." Not led. Coming, under their own power, in the present tense. By the end of his first stanza he has borrowed Keats's exact verb a second time and handed it to artillery instead of an animal: "those brute guns lowing at the skies." Whatever protection an urn gives a sacrifice, a chateau garden on the Western Front offers none.

sections.heading: The Road the Flowers Were Growing Beside
sections.body:
Vlamertinghe was the last village before Ypres, sitting on the road up from Poperinge that accounts of the [Battle of Passchendaele](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Passchendaele) describe running through a defile, "easily observed from the ridge" the Germans held above it — one of the main routes British troops used moving up to the salient. For most of the war it sat just outside German shell range, which is the only reason a chateau and its garden could still be standing there in July 1917, however far the front itself had moved from anything a garden could survive.

The date in Blunden's title puts him on that road the same month his own battalion, the 11th (Service) Battalion, Royal Sussex Regiment, went into the opening of the offensive that became known as Passchendaele. The attack began at 3:50 a.m. on 31 July 1917. That day, fighting near St Julien a few miles further up the same road, Blunden came back from a [captured pillbox](https://sites.utexas.edu/ransomcentermagazine/2010/08/17/edmund-blundens-souvenir-world-war-i-map-st-julien-belgium-july-31-1917/) with a German staff map and wrote his own note across it: "German map brought back by me from pillbox near St. Julien in the battle of July 31, 1917." The flowerbeds in this poem and the ground Passchendaele would swallow that autumn were a single road apart.

sections.heading: A Sonnet a Trench Word Breaks Open
sections.body:
Count the lines and this is a sonnet — fourteen of them, split eight and six like a classical octave and sestet. What it does with that inheritance is another matter. Into diction built to carry Keats's "mysterious priest" and "green altar," Blunden drops "gone West," soldiers' slang for dying that historians of [trench language](https://www.presenthistory.co.uk/trench-talk-slang-and-banter-in-ww1.html) group with "getting it" and "copping it" — ways of naming death, as one account of that vocabulary puts it, "without having to directly deal with it." He drops "death and lice," the second word no metaphor but the literal condition of front-line trenches. And in the second stanza he drops "mate" — addressed to nobody in Keats, because Keats's poem addresses no one at all.

The form holds. The vocabulary doesn't. Somewhere between the mansion's "queenly face" and a soldier turning mid-line to speak to the man next to him, the sonnet stops being able to keep its two languages apart.

sections.heading: The Joke at the End
sections.body:
The poem's last move isn't to say what the flowers mean. It complains about their colour: "But if you ask me, mate, the choice of colour / Is scarcely right; this red should have been duller." Poppies "by the million" on a First World War battlefield are about as worked-over an image as the war produced; Blunden doesn't reach for what they symbolise. He treats the red as a decorating mistake, the wrong shade for the setting, and leaves the reader to supply the shade it should have been.

That deflection matches what's recorded of Blunden himself. He was known for exactly this kind of dry self-deprecation, and for a physical smallness that, by his [own account](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edmund_Blunden), may have made him "an inconspicuous target" — his own half-joking explanation for surviving nearly two years at the front without a physical wound, a run that ended when he was gassed in October 1917. The Military Cross citation from earlier that year credits him in flatter language with having "displayed great courage and determination when in charge of a carrying party under heavy fire." Given the choice, Blunden reached for the joke instead.

sections.heading: A War Writer's Whole Method, in Fourteen Lines
sections.body:
Paul Fussell's 1975 study *[The Great War and Modern Memory](https://global.oup.com/academic/product/the-great-war-and-modern-memory-9780199971954)* examines Blunden alongside Siegfried Sassoon, Robert Graves, David Jones, Isaac Rosenberg and Wilfred Owen, and gives one chapter, "Arcadian Recourses," to a habit he traces through British writing on the war: reaching for the vocabulary of English pastoral tradition inside experience that tradition was never built to describe. Blunden — who titled his first two postwar collections *The Waggoner* and *The Shepherd* — is one of the writers that chapter has in view.

"Vlamertinghe: Passing the Chateau" fits that pattern without needing Fussell to have written about this specific poem. A real garden, a real chateau, a road soldiers were using that same month to reach the opening of Passchendaele, dressed from its first borrowed line in Keats's high classical language of ceremony and sacrifice. The poem never resolves the mismatch. It ends on a complaint about paint colour instead, and leaves the reader to work out exactly why the red is wrong.
